The effect of the acoustic environment of learning spaces on
students’ learning efficiency: A review
Chao Liua, Qiuyun Zangb,*, Jiaxin Lib, Xue Panb, Haoru Daib, Weijun Gaoa
aInnovation Institute for Sustainable Maritime Architecture Research and Technology, Qingdao University of Technology, China
bCollege of Architecture and Urban Planning, Qingdao University of Technology, China
A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Keywords: Numerous studies have demonstrated that the significant impact of sound on people’s perfor-
Acoustic environment in learning spaces mance, especially in mental and physical health. With a focus on students’ learning environments,
Sound pressure level this study aimed to explore the effects of different acoustic environments on students’ learning
Reverberation time efficiency. This study reviews the relevant literature on the effects of sound on learning efficiency
Learning efficiency in school and home-based learning environments since 2000. It specifically focuses on the effects
of sound sources, sound pressure level, and reverberation time on students’ learning efficiency
across all school ages. A total of 67 pieces of literature met the criteria. Firstly, the literature is
classified according to sound types, and the task types, experimental design are also presented.
Then the effects of different acoustic environments on students’ learning efficiency are summa-
rized and compared. It has been found that the impact of different sound source types on learning
efficiency varies significantly. There are clear changes under noise and variable effects in non-
noise environments. Sound pressure level has a negative impact on learning efficiency, and this
impact increases significantly when the sound environment exceeds a certain decibel level.
Studies on reverberation time often overlook the limitations of background sound and its
placement. The study proposes potential research and development directions in response to
current research. It also suggests improvement strategies for architectural design, combined with
the conclusions. This study may provide theoretical support for enhancing the learning envi-
ronment and improving learning efficiency, as well as serving as a reference for similar experi-
mental designs.
1. Introduction
In recent years, there has been a growing public concern regarding overall quality and significance of the acoustic environment.
Studies have shown that humans spend more than 90 % of their time indoors [1]. Acoustic characteristics are the primary environ-
mental factors that influence indoor satisfaction [2], and acoustic satisfaction has the most significant impact on overall satisfaction
[3]. Currently, studies on indoor acoustics are increasing and these studies cover a wide range of aspects, such as education [4–7],
health [8–16], psychological well-being [17–21], and urban architectural design [22–26]. These studies aim to investigate the rela-
tionship between indoor acoustic environments and human perception and performance.
Sound affects people’s physical and psychological health. Mental stress and psychological problems are caused by noisy envi-
ronments, and excessive noise can make people more irritable and nervous [27]. Noise, especially indoor noise (speech) [14], road

the risk of cardiovascular disease [10,12] and metabolic disease [8,9,11]. Moreover, long-term exposure to noise can also increase the
risk of developing cardiometabolic and other diseases. In contrast, being exposed to some positive sound environments, such as natural
ambient sounds and music, can greatly alleviate mental health [28], sleep quality [29–32], and physiological stress [33–35]. This can
reduce the risk of physical health problems.
Learning efficiency is an expression of how quickly or slowly one learns, encompassing accuracy, speed, comprehension, and other
factors. It is an important criterion for assessing students’ cognitive abilities and task performance. Usually, experiments assess
learning efficiency through task tests, with reading, memory, and math tests being the most common [36]. As policies and research
focus on student learning, an increasing number of scholars have begun to explore the effects of acoustic environments on students’
learning efficiency. An earlier article [4] focused on the effects of traffic noise, speech sounds, and speech intelligibility on children’s
academic performance. Klatte [37] summarized studies on the acute and chronic effects of noise exposure on children’s auditory and
non-auditory tasks, but only focused on traffic noise and irrelevant speech. Clark [38] reviewed the cognitive effects of environmental
noise (road traffic, aircraft, train, and railroad noise). However, the research mentioned above only identified studies about children.
Vaughn [39] reviewed the relationship between music and math, while Odette [40] examined the effects of different types of noise on
non-native listening. However, these studies only addressed a specific type of task. Although the review of Clark’s [41] study had a
broader focus, it did not provide a detailed analysis of different cognitive abilities as outcomes. Thompson [42] conducted a
meta-analysis of studies on noise pollution and human cognition, which included a wide range of cognitive tests (reading, mathe-
matics, attention, and memory). The study also examined different populations, including children, adolescents, and adults. However,
Thompson’s study only focused on traffic noise and speech. The number of current review studies on sound and learning efficiency is
relatively high, but the content of each one is not comprehensive. Whether studying populations, sound types, or task tests, existing
reviews focus on a single topic and lack a comprehensive summary. It is difficult to systematically summarize the effects of sound.
Therefore, this paper provides provide an updated review of the literature, expanding on the study population (from kindergarten
to university), the range of sounds, and the types of tested tasks. In order to better understand the effects of the acoustic environment in
learning spaces on student learning and to inform relevant experimental practice.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Scope of the review
The review sought to identify original research papers published from 2000 to July 2023 (research data could not be found during
the pandemic period (the first case was 17 November 2019 (3 years, 7 months and 29 days) as it was remote home education) on the
effects of acoustic environment on students’ learning efficiency. The scope of the review covered acoustic factors of sound sources
(traffic noise, irrelevant speech, natural environment sound, music), sound pressure level, and reverberation time. The study design
included both cross-sectional and longitudinal components. The task tested in the experiment are varied, as shown in Table 1. The
research literature was obtained from ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and Web of Science.
2.2. Review search strategy and review process
Papers were written in English or translated into English. The keywords searched for (Sound source, sound pressure level,
reverberation time, learning efficiency) must be in the title, abstract or keywords of papers. The reference lists of identified papers were
checked for further relevant citations. During the review process of papers, the full text of papers needs to be read and screened ac-
cording to the following criteria:
⋅ Compliance with PICOS principles (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Study Design).
⋅ Experimental sounds are frequently used and continuous.
⋅ Experimental articles have at least one cognitive test.
⋅ Experimental results have 95 % confidence intervals, or there is sufficient data provided to calculate and verify the experimental
results.
2.3. Data extraction
This systematic review extracts and verifies the following information from each eligible study based on original records: article
title, author, publication journal, publication year, research purpose, research population, age and gender of participants, inclusion
criteria, research environment, noise characteristics (type of noise exposure, noise level, reverberation time), methods for measuring
task performance, results of task performance evaluation, statistical analysis, and experimental conclusions. We rigorously screen and
tabulate data extractions throughout the process.

Based on the aforementioned selection criteria, a total of 67 eligible articles were chosen for systematic review in this paper. Fig. 1
shows the filtered data on the effects of the acoustic environment (including source type, sound pressure level, and reverberation time)
on learning efficiency. Over the past 20 years, research on the impact of sound on learning efficiency has steadily increased, with the
number of studies peaking in 2010. The overall research is primarily based on experiments, supplemented by questionnaires and other
assessment tests.
3. The effect of sound sources on students’ learning efficiency
3.1. The effect of traffic noise on students’ learning efficiency
The review included 17 experimental studies of considering the effect of traffic noise on learning efficiency [43–59] (see
Appendix A), and brief classification is shown in Table .2; 11 were tested on reading comprehension, 10 on memory tasks, only 3 on
math tasks, and the others primarily focused on listening. Studies have covered primary, middle school, and university samples.
Studies related to aircraft noise have used real scene sounds, while studies of road traffic noise have mostly relied on audio.
Schools and residences in cities are susceptible to road traffic noise [4]. Wen [60], through research with students, found that traffic
noise is the most annoying sound. In addition, numerous studies have proven that road traffic noise has a detrimental effect on learning
efficiency. For example, road traffic noise reduces reading speed [43] and calculation accuracy [44]. It also has a significant negative
effect on students’ English listening performance [45]. In terms of memory, Hygge [46] studied the effect of road traffic noise on
delayed recall and found that traffic noise can significantly impair students’ ability to recall and recognize text. While Meng [47] found
that road traffic noise can effectively shorten the reaction time of search memory and promote visual cognitive work. This may be due
to the cognitive abilities and attitudes of the individuals involved, which can result in resistance to noise interference [61].
Besides road traffic noise, some schools or homes are also affected by railroad noise [48] or aircraft noise [49]. These types of traffic
noise have a greater impact on students than road traffic noise, and among them, aircraft noise has the most significant detrimental
effect [48]. It was found that there were significant negative effects between aircraft noise and reading ability [48], as well as language
learning [52]. In addition, long-term exposure to aircraft noise has a much greater impact and is difficult to recover from, even with
adaptation. Haines [53] and Shield [54] concluded that long-term exposure to traffic noise has a negative effect on children’s cognitive
abilities. Stansfeld [55] reached the conclusion that there is a significant association between long-term exposure to aircraft noise and
reduced reading comprehension. This conclusion was drawn after testing elementary school students near airports in the Netherlands,
Spain, and the United Kingdom. Furthermore, the association remained unchanged even after making full adjustments. While other
studies found there was no significant correlation between long-term exposure to aircraft noise and decreased reading comprehension
scores [56,57], although the score was significantly lower in reading comprehension than learners who were not exposed to the same
intensity of noise [52]. Despite this, all of these studies all concluded that chronic exposure to aircraft noise was associated with poorer
sustained attention and higher levels of children. These findings further support the notion that chronic exposure to aircraft noise has a
detrimental effect on learning performance.
In summary, both road traffic noise and aircraft noise have a negative impact on students’ learning efficiency. Long-term exposure
to traffic noise has more detrimental effects, including difficulties in learning [58] and in recovering [59]. In cognitive tests, studies on
mathematics are weak, and the review conclusion was based on two cross-sectional studies with insufficient evidence of the effects of
road traffic noise on students’ mathematical abilities. Therefore, it is necessary to strengthen the experimental studies in mathematics.

Hygge [48] conducted a noise experiment with children aged 12–14 and found that speech did not affect recognition or recall. But
they reached the opposite conclusion in a new study. The study found that high school students’ recall score is lower in the presence of
irrelevant speech compared to a quiet environment, and there is a significant correlation. Irrelevant speech can also decrease the
average speed on search and memory tasks. The meaningful irrelevant speech can affect students’ memory of the text [46,62]. This is
because understandable speech leads to increased annoyance and distraction [63], which in turn decreases the accuracy and efficiency
of verbal reasoning and memory [64]. In addition, reading [65] and writing [66] can also be affected by understandable speech.
Shield’s [54] study suggested that long-term exposure can have a negative impact on the academic performance and achievement of
primary school students. Irrelevant speech causes even more disturbance than that caused by traffic noise [44,67,68].
In the context of speech sounds, the choice of sound material is often based on its contrasting and diverse possibilities. Elliott [69]
designed sound experiments using high-frequency words and low-frequency words and found no significant difference between the
two sounds. Dockrell’s [70] study set up a quiet environment, with noise generated by children alone, including classroom babble,
babble plus environmental noise, babble and environmental. It was found that students performed the worst in classroom babble and
the best in babble and environmental when performing verbal tasks (reading, spelling) as well as arithmetic tests. When students
performed non-verbal tasks (information processing), classroom babble was significantly lower compared to a quiet environment. This
was observed in terms of both the accuracy and speed of processing information. Little [71] studied the effect of background noise,
specifically different speech sounds, on recall. The results of the study not only confirmed the interference of speech on recall [36,72,
73], but also found that the effect of changing words on recall was more detrimental than repeating words. Additionally, the study
observed that the word condition was less accurate compared to pitch changes. Compared to pitch changes, the word condition was
less accurate. This also suggests that babble has a similar speech condition with changing words, which induces learned helplessness,
increases task time [65], and decreases task accuracy [47].
In summary, the presence of background speech adversely affects cognitive performance and subjective distraction. It can also
reduce short-term memory and working memory, as well as the subjective perception of noise effects. However, studies have been
unable to rule out the effects produced by knowledge deficits [74].In fact, some studies have found that if the task or test is very
complex, the presence of background speech does not affect performance [75]. It is certainly important to pay attention to the effects
caused by the research subjects [76], especially in terms of gender [77], personality [78] and age [72].
3.3. The effect of natural environment sound on students’ learning efficiency
The review included 7 studies of considering the effect of natural environment sound on learning efficiency [47,63,67,79–82] (see
Appendix C), and brief classification is shown in Table .4; 4 used natural environment sounds as masking sounds. These studies all used
laboratory audio equipment for sound settings and primarily selected spring water sound. This is because spring water sound can better
mask road traffic noise and architectural noise [83].
In general, students are less exposed to natural environments during school, so most studies have used natural sounds to mask
indoor noise. Haapakangas [79] found that the spring water sound was the most effective speech masker, based on students’ per-
formance and subjective evaluation. Zhang [80] also found that the acoustic satisfaction and accuracy of the spring water sound were
highest, and the task interference was lowest under the medium and large signal-to-noise ratio conditions. However, Lee [81] found
that people had the worst overall cognitive scores and the lowest levels of satisfaction when exposed to spring water sound. Since the
perception of sound is complex and often influenced by various factors, such as individual personalities, environmental conditions, and
specific tasks. It is necessary to pay careful attention to the details of the environment in order to achieve the same positive effects of
spring water masking sounds in different learning environments.
In terms of the relationship between natural sounds and learning efficiency, Liu [63] found that students had higher accuracy and
efficiency when exposed to the sound of spring water compared to noise. It means natural environment sounds have a positive impact
on learning efficiency. Song [82] found that students’ attention levels were slightly higher in natural sound environments (a mixed
sound of valley water and birds in a forest) than in traffic noise. However, Meng’s [47] study found that spring water sound signif-
icantly interfered with the students’ visual cognitive and location memory performance compared to the control group (quiet envi-
ronment). This interference was second only to the negative effect caused by irrelevant speech. In addition, the spring water can

3.4. The effect of music on students’ learning efficiency
The review included 14 studies of considering the effect of music on learning efficiency [39,47,63,67,78,84–92] (see Appendix D),
and a brief classification is shown in Table .5; 3 were tested on reading comprehension, 6 on memory tasks, 3 on math tasks. These
studies all used laboratory audio equipment for sound settings.
Studies have concluded that learning music has a positive effect on math scores [39] and verbal memory [84]. However, when used
as a background sound for learning, there is no consensus on the impact of music on task performance. Hall [85] divided the students
into two groups: a music group and a no-music group for the reading tests. Compared to the no-music group, nearly 58 % of the
students in the music group showed improvement in their scores, with an average increase of 2.37 %. Meng [47] found that music can
increase reaction speed, effectively shortening reaction time compared to a quiet environment. However, Iwanaga [67] found that
music can reduce students’ ability to pay attention and verbalize their memory. It suggests that music, like noise, may interfere with
the processing of verbal information, reduce subjects’ task performance [78,86,87], and increase brain load [88]. However, it is
worthwhile to recognize that the effect of music sound is weaker compared to noise [63].
In terms of music selection, scholars typically choose music with strong contrasts, placing emphasis on factors such as familiarity,
genre, and emotional content. Chew [87] studied the impact of music familiarity and found that scores on reading comprehension and
arithmetic tasks were the lowest when participants were exposed to unfamiliar songs. It suggests that familiar music inhibits cognitive
recognition [89]. In terms of music genres, Liu [63] compared the effects of pure classical music and classical music with lyrics on
students’ attention and verbal reasoning skills. It was found that pure classical music is more effective in improving students’ attention
and verbal reasoning abilities. Whereas pop music with lyrics [88] leads to more distraction and reduces verbal memory [67]. In
addition, the emotional content of music can also have an impact on learning [86]. Positive music can enhance students’ behavior to a
certain extent [90], while negative music can be a significant distraction and reduce task performance [91].
In summary, current research on music is not yet completely certain about its effect on learning efficiency. Music can enhance
learning, but it may also create noise-like interference. In addition, certain fundamental aspects of music, such as melody and rhythm
[93], distinctions between lyrics and instrumental music [88], continuity of the music [92], familiarity with the music [87], and even
the type of task [78], may negatively affect learning efficiency.
4. The effect of sound pressure level on students’ learning efficiency
The intensity of sound in the learning environment can affect learning efficiency. The review included 13 studies of considering the
effect of sound pressure level (SPL) on learning efficiency [45,48,49,54,63,68,88,90,94–98] (see Appendix E), and a brief classification
is shown in Table .6; 6 were tested on reading comprehension, 4 on memory tasks, 2 on math tasks. These studies all used laboratory
audio equipment for sound settings and the SPL of the experimental sound was mostly in increments of 10 dBA or 15dBA.
In general, there is a significant negative correlation between SPL and students’ learning efficiency. The higher SPL, the greater the
interference level of noise on students, resulting in lower the learning efficiency and accuracy [54], as well as increased annoyance
[45] among students. High noise levels can degrade reading performance [94]. Liu [88] compared the reading comprehension per-
formance of university students under different SPL of 45, 65, and 85 dBA. The study found that the reading performance of university
students was the best at 45 dBA, followed by 65 dBA and 85 dBA. In memory tests, high noise levels can impair students’ memory [95].
Hygge [48] found that students’ mean scores on the recall test decreased with increasing SPL in the same sound condition. The highest
scores were observed in the quiet environment (44 dBA). However, there was no significant difference in scores for the three SPL on
text recognition. In addition, high levels of noise also have a negative impact on attention [49] and verbal reasoning tests [63].
Furthermore, the negative effects become more pronounced when the noise exceed 50 dBA. In terms of subjective evaluation, Huang
[96] found that students were satisfied with the acoustic environment when noise levels were below 49.6 dBA. When the noise level

Studies in recent years have shown that the impact of SPL on students’ learning efficiency is not determined by a single factor, but
rather the result of multiple factors. Zhang [68] found a statistically significant two-way interaction between sound pressure level and
sound type on children (p =0.002). It suggests that noise can contribute to the harm caused by sound pressure level and increase the
error rate on cognitive tests [97]. In addition, age and task testing also have an effect. Connolly [98] found that older students were
more susceptible to the noise, while younger students did not show a consistent pattern. In fact, some younger students even performed
better in certain tests conducted at 64 dBA. Zhang [97] found that younger students were more affected by noise. The tendency of
students’ performance in different task tests was inconsistent across age groups.
In summary, regardless of whether the effect of sound pressure level (SPL) on learning efficiency is a single factor or interacts with
other conditions, the results are unambiguous. Learning performance consistently decreases with increasing SPL. However, there are
still other influencing factors in the experiment. Therefore, the regularity of interaction among age, task difficulty, and sound pressure
level still needs to be studied in depth.
5. The effect of reverberation time on students’ learning efficiency
The review included 13 studies considering the effect of reverberation time (RT) on learning efficiency [45,99–110] (see
Appendix F), and a brief classification is shown in Table .7; 2 were tested on reading comprehension, 6 on memory tasks, 1 on math
tasks. The experimental sound was adjusted by room acoustic materials or software simulations.
In general, the shorter the RT, the drier the sound, and the longer the RT, the more mixed the sound. When the RT is long, the mixed
sound can blur the actual sound environment, making it difficult for listeners to accurately recognize speech [99–101]. Studies have
generally concluded that prolonged RT has a negative impact on cognition [102], impairing speech perception [103], decreasing
memory for language [104], and even increasing reaction time [105]. However, Perham [106] found that the sound did not signif-
icantly impair the memory ability under two RT conditions (0.7s, 0.9s).
The experimental tests in the aforementioned studies were directly related to the background sound. Background sound, when used
as a material for task testing, can be generated through prolonged reverberation, resulting in a reduction in speech intelligibility [111].
This, in turn, impacts the efficiency of task testing. Whereas, when the background sound was irrelevant, there was a positive effect of
reverberation time on task performance. Beaman [107] examined the effect of a reverberant auditory environment on immediate recall
through two experiments. In the simulated environment, the auditory environment with reverberation produced less interference than
the one without reverberation. In addition, certain acoustic factors can interact with RT. For example, the RT and the maximum
background noise level work together to affect students’ academic performance [108]. Chen [45] found that RT had a significant
impact on the objective performance of the subjects when the traffic noise level was 50 dBA. At other sound pressure level conditions
(TNL =40, 45, and 55 dBA), changes in reverberation time had little effect on the accuracy of subjects and their cognitive impairment.
In addition, Hurtig [109] found that longer RT (1.2s) impaired memory when the signal-to-noise ratio was +12 dB. However, longer
RT improved children’s memory when the signal-to-noise ratio was +3 dB.
In summary, the reverberation time can decrease the intelligibility of language. In self-study rooms, having a relatively long RT has
a positive impact on learning efficiency. However, during daily classes, it is necessary to shorten the RT in order to improve the
intelligibility of the classroom space and increase the efficiency of students’ learning [110]. In addition, we found that a large number
of current studies only focus on RT. Although the importance of background sound has been acknowledged, there are very few studies
on speech transmission index (STI), which is a significant shortcoming in current research.
6. Engineering practices to enhance the acoustic environment of learning spaces
The proposed standard for background noise in learning spaces, particularly classrooms, in developed countries is 35 dBA. In China,
the background noise requirement is set at 40–45 dBA due to the influence of urban population and building density. The reverberation
time (RT) setting depends on the volume of the learning space. A common range for the acoustic environment adaptation in learning
spaces is standardized at 0.4–0.8s, with 0.6s being the most prevalent [112]. When designing or remodeling learning spaces, we pay
attention to making adjustments to their acoustic environment.
At present, several studies have suggested measures to improve the quality of the acoustic environment in learning spaces. This
paper briefly summarizes the relevant strategies for improvement, which can be broadly divided into three aspects. Firstly, noise can
be reduced by adjusting the layout during the design process. For external noise, Wen [60] studied the impact of urban traffic on the

acoustic comfort of school classrooms located near roadsides. They suggested that schools should be located as far away as possible

suggests that reducing speech interference is possible by designing an open floor plan to increase the reverberation time (RT) of the
indoor space. Secondly, the building facade components can be renovated. A significant number of practices have chosen to replace
windows in order to improve their acoustic performance by enhancing their airtightness [113]. Balasbaneh [114] conducted a sus-
tainability assessment of single, double, and triple-pane windows and found that triple-pane windows offered the highest level of
acoustic insulation. However, taking into account factors such as cost, it was concluded that double-pane windows were the most
sustainable choice for school buildings. Of course, other components of the exterior facade, such as shading components [115], are
capable of providing some noise reduction. Alternatively, sound impacts can be effectively reduced by using acoustic materials. Zhang
[68] conducted a study where acoustic panels were added to the walls and ceilings of classrooms in order to reduce the reverberation
time in the room. Sadick [116] discovered that renovated schools with acoustic materials on ceilings and floors was more effective in
improving indoor acoustic comfort compared to new schools. It was also found that placing acoustic materials on the back wall was
more effective than placing them on the ceiling [112].
These improvement strategies mainly focus on reducing the sound pressure level and reverberation time, which effect cannot be
ignored. They can effectively reduce background noise in the learning environment, improve indoor comfort, and create an optimal
learning environment for students.
7. Conclusions
This review examines the relationship between the acoustic environment in learning spaces and students’ learning efficiency, based
on previous studies. This paper has several strengths and contributions. The strength of this review is quite comprehensive. The study’s
sound environment is diverse, encompassing various types of sound sources (traffic noise, irrelevant speech, natural environment
sounds, and music). The review also considers factors such as sound pressure level and reverberation time, providing a multidi-
mensional assessment of the impact of sound on learning efficiency. The study population is broad, ranging from kindergarten to
university, which enhances the objectivity of the summary characteristics. Furthermore, the review covers a wide range of test content,
primarily focusing on reading comprehension, memory, and mathematical calculation. At least two researchers were responsible for
each stage of paper selection in the article selection process, following a standardized protocol for systematic review. For this
contribution, the paper refines existing research on the relationship between the sound environment and learning efficiency. It also
provides a brief summary of practical strategies for improving the acoustic environment in learning places, and discusses potential
improvements and future directions. It is of practical significance to improve the learning environment and enhance the quality of
learning.
7.1. Summary
(1) Sound sources: The research results of sound sources are quite varied. Traffic noise and speech significantly interfere with
learning efficiency. Long-term exposure to aircraft noise can even impair students’ attention and behavioral skills, making
recovery difficult. Background speech, especially intelligible speech, is more detrimental to memory. It is worth noting that
some studies have found that speech-induced interference is greater, but it has not been conclusively confirmed. The impact of
natural environment sounds and music on learning efficiency is not clear. Natural environment sounds have both advantages
and disadvantages when used as masking or background sounds. The conclusions about music are also inconsistent. It has been
found to improve accuracy on task tests, on the one hand. It can have a distracting effect on students due to its inherent rhythmic
properties or the presence of lyric, which can be as distracting as intelligible speech), on the other hand. Therefore, when
designing the internal acoustics of a self-study room, it should be designed to ensure a quiet environment as much as possible. In
addition, music can be used appropriately to mask other noises.
(2) Sound pressure levels: The research results on the impact of sound pressure level on learning efficiency are relatively clear.
Students’ learning efficiency decreases significantly as the sound pressure level increases in the same sound environment. This
indicates that a lower sound pressure level is more beneficial for learning. However, the relationship between sound pressure
level and learning efficiency is not simple linear. When the sound environment exceeds 50 dBA, the decreasing trend becomes
more pronounced. Therefore, this conclusion can provide some references for the design of sound insulation in buildings. For
example, external window glazing or interior soundproofing materials can be selected based on the noise level of local traffic
roads.
(3) Reverberation time: The study of reverberation time is not sufficient and is often constrained by some factors. Many studies
have established scenarios in which students study independently instead of listening to lectures. In these scenarios, a longer
reverberation time has a positive impact on learning efficiency. This is because longer reverberation can blur the surrounding
sounds, making the noise less clear and the speech less understandable. Thus, it can reduce the disturbance to the students.
Therefore, self-study rooms can be designed with an open floor plan to effectively increase RT in order to minimize noise
(speech) disruptions and enhance learning productivity.
7.2. Potential research
Based on the existing literature research, it can be found that there is still a lack of clear or sufficient research on three aspects:
sound source, sound pressure level, and reverberation time. There are also significant gaps in the experiment design. Therefore, further
research should be conducted on the following points:

(1) Enhancing research on sound sources: Long-term exposure to traffic noise, natural environment sound, and music should be
further studied. The relationship between long-term traffic noise exposure and learning efficiency in current studies is not clear,
and most studies have chosen aircraft noise as the background sound. However, there are few studies on long-term exposure to
road traffic noise in a wide range of schools and homes, making it difficult to draw accurate conclusions about its effects on
students’ learning efficiency. In addition, the relationship between sound and learning efficiency, both in natural environment
sound and music, is of mixed merit. Especially when it comes to the various music styles, reaching an accurate conclusion can be
challenging. The relationship between music and quiet environments is even more difficult to compare. Therefore, the un-
certainty surrounding the relationship between these sounds and learning efficiency provides a foundation and guidance for
future research.
(2) Avoiding irrelevant factors: Future research should more clearly separate acoustic conditions from other disturbing factors. In
some experiments, a noise-free environment was selected as the control group, while a noise environment was used to adjust the
sound pressure level strength for analysis. Alternatively, some experiments were affected by inconsistencies in the difficulty of
the selected task tests, as well as significant variations in subjects’ age, gender, and personality. These factors introduced the risk
of confounding the study findings with multiple variables. When the difficulty of the topic is high, there is often little difference
in the experimental results among the subjects. Although the current research suggests that traffic noise, irrelevant speech, and
sound pressure levels have a negative effect on learning efficiency, it is challenging to determine the extent of these changes and
the significance of their impact are significant in the presence of multiple factors. Therefore, future studies should further
consider the role of sound conditions (musical rhythm, musical mood, as well as whether the sound is intermittent), task dif-
ficulty, and individual characteristics (gender, personality, age, musical familiarity, and noise sensitivity) in order to minimize
the impact of irrelevant factors on experimental results.
(3) Enhancing research on speech intelligibility: Studies related to speech intelligibility in the room needs to be enhanced in the
future. Reverberation time plays an important role in classroom design and directly affects the sound quality and speech
intelligibility in the classroom. However, when considering reverberation time in realistic scenarios, there is also a need to
evaluate the background noise level in the room, which is a limitation in current research. It is well known that the speech
transmission index (STI) is the best single descriptor of room acoustics. It measures the quality and intelligibility of speech
transmission. A reliable STI metric can assist individuals in accurately perceiving and comprehending speech. This is a crucial
factor to consider when designing acoustic environment for classroom. Currently, there are limited studies on STI. Even the
results of reverberation time research are uncertain. Therefore, future research in this field should be strengthened, not only
limited to self-study classrooms, but also involving lecture classrooms, in order to obtain accurate design criteria for indoor
acoustic environments.
(4) Determining a sound evaluation standard: It is necessary to establish a unified and reliable sound evaluation standard. There
are many rubrics available for assessing learning efficiency in current research. These rubrics tend to place a greater focus on
reading comprehension and memory, while giving less attention to math. Attention and listening are also the main focus of
current research. However, no conclusions have been reached regarding about the relationship between any acoustic envi-
ronment and tasks, making it difficult to determine the cognitive performance weight attributed to each task. In addition, the
experimental procedures and the analysis of the results are quite different. Although scientific development requires innovation,
excessively novel methods often prevent studies from directly comparing and drawing conclusions for quantitative analysis,
resulting in heterogeneity of findings. If there is a unified research method and evaluation index, it could greatly advance this
field of research. Therefore, in follow-up studies, it would be beneficial to standardize the methods used in this research field.
This would involve seeking the same test content, using consistent evaluation and statistical analysis methods as previous or
contemporary studies. By doing so, the research results can be directly compared, leading to more accurate and comprehensive
quantitative conclusions.
(5) Adding physiological indicators: Future research could incorporate other metrics. During the literature screening, we found a
large number of studies that only conducted cognitive tests. Some studies combined with subjective evaluations, while very few
studies utilized physiological indicators (blood pressure, heart rate variability, skin conductance, MRI, EEG). With the inte-
gration of multiple disciplines, studies incorporating physiology have gradually increased in recent years. In the future, the
utilization of physiological indicators should be further enhanced to effectively measure experimental outcomes and provide
strong evidence.
